sub_obligations.plain_summary: For cross-border processing, the supervisory authority where the company has its main or only EU establishment acts as the lead regulator.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy identify a specific lead supervisory authority (tied to the company's main or single EU establishment) for its cross-border processing?

sub_obligations.legal_text: The lead supervisory authority shall be the sole interlocutor of the controller or processor for the cross-border processing carried out by that controller or processor
sub_obligations.plain_summary: The company should treat the lead supervisory authority as its single point of contact for cross-border processing matters.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy indicate that the identified lead supervisory authority serves as the company's sole point of contact for cross-border processing issues?

expected_evidence: Privacy policy contact/regulator section naming the lead supervisory authority

assessment_rules.met_when: The single sub-obligation set is satisfied: the policy names a lead supervisory authority tied to the company's main/single EU establishment and treats it as the sole interlocutor for cross-border processing.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: A supervisory authority is named but it is unclear whether it corresponds to the company's main/single EU establishment, or the 'sole interlocutor' role is not made clear.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The company carries out cross-border processing but does not identify any lead supervisory authority.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy names a supervisory authority with no connection to any EU establishment of the company as its lead authority.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company's processing qualifies as cross-border, so applicability of this group cannot be determined.

article.title: Tasks
article.contextual_reason: This article enumerates the tasks each supervisory authority performs on its own territory (monitoring, public awareness, advising government, handling complaints, accreditation, adopting standard clauses, and similar regulatory functions). These are duties of the regulator itself, not of controllers or processors, so none of it is testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Powers
article.contextual_reason: This article lists the investigative, corrective, and authorisation/advisory powers supervisory authorities may exercise over controllers and processors (e.g., ordering information, auditing, issuing fines, suspending data flows). It describes what a regulator can do to a company, not an affirmative obligation the company's own policy could satisfy or fail, so it is not testable as a compliance requirement against a privacy policy.

article.title: Activity reports
article.contextual_reason: This article requires each supervisory authority to draw up and transmit an annual activity report to its national parliament, government, and other authorities. It is a reporting obligation of the regulator, not of controllers or processors, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Cooperation between the lead supervisory authority and the other supervisory authorities concerned

requirement_groups.principle: Controller/processor compliance with a one-stop-shop decision
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Once notified of the lead supervisory authority's decision, the controller or processor must take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with it across processing activities at all its EU establishments, and must notify the lead supervisory authority of the measures taken.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where a lead supervisory authority has issued a binding decision concerning the controller or processor's cross-border processing under the one-stop-shop procedure.

sub_obligations.legal_text: the controller or processor shall take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with the decision as regards processing activities in the context of all its establishments in the Union
sub_obligations.plain_summary: The company must implement the lead authority's decision across all its EU establishments, not just the one addressed.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the company's process describe implementing a lead supervisory authority's binding decision across all EU establishments' processing activities?

sub_obligations.legal_text: The controller or processor shall notify the measures taken for complying with the decision to the lead supervisory authority, which shall inform the other supervisory authorities concerned
sub_obligations.plain_summary: The company must report back to the lead authority on what it did to comply.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the company's process include notifying the lead supervisory authority of the compliance measures taken following its decision?

expected_evidence: Records of correspondence with lead supervisory authority

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: the company has a documented process for both implementing a lead authority decision EU-wide and notifying the lead authority of the measures taken.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: The company describes implementing such decisions but has no defined process for notifying the lead authority, or vice versa.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: There is no process for responding to or implementing a lead supervisory authority decision.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The company states it will only apply a lead authority's decision to the establishment directly addressed, not EU-wide.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company has ever been, or expects to be, subject to a lead supervisory authority decision.

article.title: Mutual assistance
article.contextual_reason: This article governs how supervisory authorities request and provide mutual assistance to one another. It creates no obligation for controllers or processors and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Joint operations of supervisory authorities
article.contextual_reason: This article governs joint investigations and enforcement operations between supervisory authorities, including staff secondment and liability between Member States. It creates no obligation for controllers or processors and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Consistency mechanism
article.contextual_reason: This article introduces the consistency mechanism as a framework for cooperation between supervisory authorities and the Commission. It is a structural provision with no controller or processor obligation and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Opinion of the Board
article.contextual_reason: This article governs when and how the European Data Protection Board issues opinions on draft decisions by supervisory authorities. It creates no obligation for controllers or processors and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Dispute resolution by the Board
article.contextual_reason: This article governs how the Board adopts binding decisions to resolve disputes between supervisory authorities. It creates no obligation for controllers or processors and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Urgency procedure
article.contextual_reason: This article lets a supervisory authority adopt provisional measures and request urgent Board opinions or decisions in exceptional circumstances. It governs regulator-to-regulator/Board procedure, not controller or processor conduct, and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Exchange of information
article.contextual_reason: This article authorizes the Commission to adopt implementing acts specifying electronic information-exchange arrangements between supervisory authorities and the Board. It creates no obligation for controllers or processors and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: European Data Protection Board
article.contextual_reason: This article establishes the European Data Protection Board, its legal personality, and its composition. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Independence
article.contextual_reason: This article requires the Board to act independently. It is an institutional provision governing the Board, not controllers or processors, and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Tasks of the Board
article.contextual_reason: This article lists the Board's own tasks, such as issuing guidelines, advising the Commission, accrediting certification bodies, and maintaining registers. These are duties of the Board, not of controllers or processors, and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Reports
article.contextual_reason: This article requires the Board to draw up and publish an annual report. It is a Board reporting duty, not a controller or processor obligation, and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Procedure
article.contextual_reason: This article sets the Board's internal voting and rules-of-procedure requirements. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Chair
article.contextual_reason: This article governs election and term of the Board's Chair and deputy chairs. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Tasks of the Chair
article.contextual_reason: This article lists the duties of the Board's Chair, such as convening meetings and notifying decisions. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Secretariat
article.contextual_reason: This article establishes the Board's secretariat, provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor, and its administrative functions. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Confidentiality
article.contextual_reason: This article governs confidentiality of Board discussions and access to Board documents under EU public-access rules. It is purely institutional and creates no controller or processor obligation testable against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority

requirement_groups.principle: Disclosure of the right to complain to a supervisory authority
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Data subjects have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, particularly in the Member State of their habitual residence, place of work, or place of the alleged infringement, if they consider the processing of their data infringes the GDPR.

sub_obligations.legal_text: every data subject shall have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement
sub_obligations.plain_summary: People can complain to a data protection authority, generally one connected to where they live, work, or where the issue occurred.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy inform data subjects of their right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, including in their Member State of residence, work, or where the alleged infringement occurred?

expected_evidence: Contact details for relevant supervisory authorities

assessment_rules.met_when: The single sub-obligation is satisfied: the policy clearly informs data subjects of their right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: The right to complain is mentioned but without any indication of which authorities may be relevant (e.g., residence-based option).
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The policy does not mention the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority at all.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy states or implies that data subjects may not complain to a supervisory authority, or must first pursue other remedies exclusively.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: No rights section or equivalent disclosure is available for review.

article.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a supervisory authority
article.contextual_reason: This article gives individuals a judicial remedy against a supervisory authority's decisions or inaction. It concerns the relationship between a data subject and the regulator or courts, not any action or disclosure by the controller or processor, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor

requirement_groups.principle: Disclosure of the right to a judicial remedy and applicable venue
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Data subjects have the right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor where they consider their GDPR rights have been infringed, and such proceedings may be brought in the Member State of the controller/processor's establishment or, generally, the data subject's habitual residence.

sub_obligations.legal_text: each data subject shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy where he or she considers that his or her rights under this Regulation have been infringed
sub_obligations.plain_summary: People can go to court against the company if they believe their GDPR rights were violated.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy inform data subjects of their right to an effective judicial remedy against the controller or processor?

sub_obligations.legal_text: Proceedings against a controller or a processor shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the controller or processor has an establishment. Alternatively, such proceedings may be brought before the courts of the Member State where the data subject has his or her habitual residence
sub_obligations.plain_summary: The lawsuit can generally be filed either where the company is established or where the person lives.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy indicate that judicial proceedings may be brought either where the company is established or where the data subject habitually resides?

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: the policy discloses the right to a judicial remedy against the company AND correctly reflects the available venue options (company establishment or, generally, data subject residence).
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: The right to a judicial remedy is disclosed but venue options are omitted or incompletely described.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The policy does not mention the right to a judicial remedy against the controller/processor at all.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy states data subjects may only sue in a jurisdiction other than the company's establishment or their own habitual residence (e.g., mandating a third-country forum without legal basis), or purports to waive this right entirely.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: No rights, remedies, or governing-law section is available for review.

requirement_groups.principle: Right to be represented by a qualifying not-for-profit body
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Data subjects may mandate a properly constituted not-for-profit body with public-interest statutory objectives in data protection to lodge complaints and exercise their Article 77, 78, and 79 rights (and Article 82 compensation rights, where Member State law allows) on their behalf.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies where the company's disclosures address how data subjects may exercise their rights, including via representation.

sub_obligations.legal_text: The data subject shall have the right to mandate a not-for-profit body, organisation or association...to lodge the complaint on his or her behalf, to exercise the rights referred to in Articles 77, 78 and 79 on his or her behalf, and to exercise the right to receive compensation referred to in Article 82 on his or her behalf where provided for by Member State law
sub_obligations.plain_summary: People can authorize a qualifying non-profit organisation to complain and pursue remedies for them, including compensation where national law permits.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy acknowledge that data subjects may mandate a qualifying not-for-profit body to lodge complaints or pursue remedies on their behalf?

expected_evidence: Privacy policy 'your rights' section referencing representation

assessment_rules.met_when: The single sub-obligation is satisfied: the policy or complaint-handling process acknowledges data subjects' right to be represented by a qualifying not-for-profit body for complaints and remedies.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: The company's complaint process would accept a representative in practice, but the policy is silent on this right.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The policy or process does not address representation at all and gives no indication a mandated body would be accommodated.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy states that complaints or rights requests will only be accepted directly from the data subject, refusing to recognize any qualifying representative.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: There is no rights or complaints section addressing how requests must be submitted.

article.title: Suspension of proceedings
article.contextual_reason: This article governs coordination between national courts handling related proceedings against the same controller or processor (contacting each other, suspending or declining jurisdiction). It regulates court procedure, not controller or processor conduct or disclosures, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

requirement_groups.principle: Disclosure of the right to compensation
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Anyone who suffers material or non-material damage from an infringement of the GDPR has the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor responsible.

sub_obligations.legal_text: Any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement of this Regulation shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor for the damage suffered
sub_obligations.plain_summary: People harmed by a GDPR violation, financially or otherwise, can claim compensation from the responsible company.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy inform data subjects of their right to compensation for material or non-material damage caused by a GDPR infringement?

assessment_rules.met_when: The single sub-obligation is satisfied: the policy discloses the right to compensation for both material and non-material damage.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: A right to compensation is mentioned but limited to only one damage type (e.g., financial loss only) or described vaguely.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The policy makes no mention of a right to compensation for GDPR infringements.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy purports to exclude or limit the right to compensation for GDPR infringements (e.g., a blanket liability waiver covering data protection claims).
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: No rights or liability section is available for review.

requirement_groups.principle: Joint and several liability among multiple controllers/processors
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Where more than one controller or processor is involved in the same processing and responsible for damage, each is liable for the entire damage to ensure effective compensation, with a right to reclaim a proportionate share from the other responsible parties.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company's processing involves multiple controllers and/or processors jointly responsible for the same processing activity (e.g., joint controller arrangements or processor chains).

sub_obligations.legal_text: each controller or processor shall be held liable for the entire damage in order to ensure effective compensation of the data subject
sub_obligations.plain_summary: In joint processing arrangements, any one responsible party can be held liable for the full damage.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where multiple controllers/processors are jointly involved, does the company's documentation acknowledge that any one of them may be held liable for the entire damage?

sub_obligations.legal_text: that controller or processor shall be entitled to claim back from the other controllers or processors involved in the same processing that part of the compensation corresponding to their part of responsibility for the damage
sub_obligations.plain_summary: A party that pays full compensation can seek reimbursement from other responsible parties for their share.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the company's joint controller or processor agreement address the right to reclaim a proportionate share of compensation paid from other responsible parties?

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: relevant agreements acknowledge full joint-and-several liability toward the data subject AND provide for proportionate reimbursement among responsible parties.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: Joint liability toward the data subject is acknowledged but internal reimbursement/apportionment terms are missing, or vice versa.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: No joint controller or processor agreement addresses liability or reimbursement despite multiple parties being involved in the same processing.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: An agreement purports to fully shield one joint party from liability to the data subject, contrary to the joint-and-several rule.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company's processing involves multiple jointly responsible controllers or processors.

article.title: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
article.contextual_reason: This article sets out the factors supervisory authorities must weigh and the fine thresholds when imposing administrative fines. It directs regulator decision-making rather than imposing a disclosure or documentary obligation on controllers or processors, so its content is not testable against a company privacy policy (the underlying substantive obligations it references, such as Articles 5-9, 12-22, 25-39, and 44-49, are separately testable under their own articles).

article.title: Penalties
article.contextual_reason: This article requires Member States to lay down rules on other penalties for infringements not covered by administrative fines and to notify the Commission accordingly. It is a Member State legislative obligation, not a controller or processor obligation, and cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Processing and freedom of expression and information
article.contextual_reason: This article requires Member States to legislate exemptions reconciling data protection with freedom of expression (journalistic, academic, artistic, literary purposes) and to notify the Commission of those laws. It is a Member State legislative obligation, not a directly testable controller or processor requirement, so it cannot be assessed against a company privacy policy.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Processing and public access to official documents
article.contextual_reason: This article permits public authorities and bodies to disclose personal data in official documents in accordance with Union or Member State access-to-documents law. It authorizes disclosure under national law rather than setting a testable requirement for a typical company's privacy policy, and applies specifically to official-document access regimes rather than general commercial processing.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Processing of the national identification number

requirement_groups.principle: Safeguards for national identification numbers
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Where a company processes a national identification number or other identifier of general application, it must use it only under appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of the data subject, consistent with any specific conditions set by the relevant Member State.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company processes a national identification number (e.g., a national ID, tax, or social security number) or other identifier of general application, and the relevant Member State has set specific conditions for its use under this Article.

sub_obligations.legal_text: the national identification number or any other identifier of general application shall be used only under appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of the data subject pursuant to this Regulation
sub_obligations.plain_summary: National ID numbers or similar identifiers must be handled with extra protective measures beyond ordinary personal data.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where the company processes a national identification number or similar general identifier, does the policy describe appropriate safeguards applied specifically to that processing?

expected_evidence: Data classification policy addressing national ID numbers
Security measures specific to identifier processing

assessment_rules.met_when: The single sub-obligation is satisfied: the policy identifies specific safeguards applied to national identification number processing.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: The company acknowledges processing national identification numbers but describes only generic (non-identifier-specific) safeguards.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The company processes a national identification number with no additional safeguards described anywhere.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy explicitly treats national identification numbers the same as any other low-sensitivity data field with no extra protection.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company processes any national identification number or general identifier.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Processing in the context of employment

requirement_groups.principle: Safeguards for employee data processing
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Where a Member State has adopted more specific employment-context rules under Article 88(1), those rules — and by extension the employer's practices under them — must include suitable and specific measures safeguarding employees' human dignity, legitimate interests, and fundamental rights, with particular regard to transparency, intra-group transfers of employee data, and workplace monitoring systems.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company processes employee personal data in an employment context (e.g., recruitment, contract performance, workforce management, health and safety, workplace monitoring) and the relevant Member State has adopted more specific rules under Article 88(1).

sub_obligations.legal_text: suitable and specific measures to safeguard the data subject's human dignity, legitimate interests and fundamental rights, with particular regard to the transparency of processing
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Employee data processing must be transparent and protect employees' dignity and fundamental rights.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the employment/HR privacy notice describe transparent processing of employee data that safeguards employees' dignity and fundamental rights?

sub_obligations.legal_text: the transfer of personal data within a group of undertakings, or a group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Where employee data is shared within a corporate group, that sharing must also be safeguarded appropriately.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where employee data is transferred within a corporate group, does the policy describe safeguards for those intra-group transfers?

sub_obligations.legal_text: monitoring systems at the work place
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Workplace monitoring systems (e.g., email, camera, activity monitoring) must be subject to specific safeguards.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where workplace monitoring systems are used, does the policy describe specific safeguards and transparency measures for that monitoring?

expected_evidence: Employee data transfer agreements within corporate group

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: the company's employment-context data practices are transparent, protect dignity and fundamental rights, and specifically address intra-group transfers and workplace monitoring where applicable.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: Some elements are addressed (e.g., a general HR privacy notice exists) but specific treatment of monitoring systems or intra-group transfers is missing.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The company processes employee data with no HR-specific privacy notice or safeguards addressing dignity, transparency, monitoring, or intra-group transfers.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The company operates workplace monitoring or intra-group employee data sharing while explicitly disclaiming any employee transparency or safeguard measures.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company processes employee personal data or whether the relevant Member State has adopted Article 88(1) rules.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Safeguards and derogations relating to processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes

requirement_groups.principle: Appropriate safeguards for archiving, research, and statistical processing
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes must be subject to appropriate technical and organisational safeguards, in particular ensuring data minimisation, with pseudonymisation used where the purpose allows, and full de-identification used wherever the purpose can still be achieved without identifying data subjects.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company processes personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes.

sub_obligations.legal_text: technical and organisational measures are in place in particular in order to ensure respect for the principle of data minimisation
sub_obligations.plain_summary: The company must have technical and organisational measures ensuring only the minimum necessary data is used for these purposes.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy describe technical and organisational measures ensuring data minimisation for archiving, research, or statistical processing?

sub_obligations.legal_text: Those measures may include pseudonymisation provided that those purposes can be fulfilled in that manner
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Pseudonymisation should be used for this processing where it doesn't prevent achieving the purpose.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy indicate that pseudonymisation is used for archiving, research, or statistical processing where feasible?

sub_obligations.legal_text: Where those purposes can be fulfilled by further processing which does not permit or no longer permits the identification of data subjects, those purposes shall be fulfilled in that manner
sub_obligations.plain_summary: If the purpose can be met using fully de-identified data, the company must process the data in that de-identified way instead.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Does the policy commit to using fully de-identified (non-identifying) data for archiving, research, or statistical purposes whenever that would still fulfil the purpose?

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: technical/organisational measures ensure data minimisation, pseudonymisation is used where feasible, and fully de-identified processing is used wherever it would still achieve the purpose.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: Some safeguards (e.g., general data minimisation) are described but pseudonymisation or preference for de-identified processing is not addressed.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: The company conducts archiving, research, or statistical processing with no described safeguards, minimisation, or pseudonymisation measures.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy states identifiable data is retained and used for these purposes even where de-identified data would suffice, contrary to the requirement.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company conducts any archiving, research, or statistical processing.

requirement_groups.principle: Derogations from certain rights for research and statistical purposes
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Where permitted by Union or Member State law, derogations from the rights to access, rectification, restriction, and objection may apply to processing for scientific or historical research or statistical purposes, but only where those rights would seriously impair achieving the purpose, only to the extent necessary, and only alongside the 89(1) safeguards.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company relies on a research/statistical-purposes derogation from data subject rights under applicable Union or Member State law.

sub_obligations.legal_text: Union or Member State law may provide for derogations from the rights referred to in Articles 15, 16, 18 and 21...in so far as such rights are likely to render impossible or seriously impair the achievement of the specific purposes, and such derogations are necessary for the fulfilment of those purposes
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Rights like access, rectification, restriction, and objection can only be limited for research/statistics if honoring them would seriously undermine the research and the limitation is necessary.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where the company limits data subject rights for research or statistical processing, does the policy confirm this is done only where such rights would seriously impair the specific purpose and only to the extent necessary, together with the safeguards required under 89(1)?

expected_evidence: Research ethics/data governance policy addressing rights derogations
Legal basis documentation citing applicable national research derogation law

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: any rights derogation for research/statistical purposes is grounded in applicable law, limited to cases of serious impairment, necessary, and paired with 89(1) safeguards.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: A derogation is applied but its legal basis, necessity, or accompanying safeguards are not clearly documented.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: Data subject rights are limited for research/statistical processing with no reference to a legal derogation or necessity test.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy applies a blanket denial of access, rectification, restriction, or objection rights to all research/statistical processing regardless of actual impact on the purpose.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company applies any rights derogation for research or statistical purposes.

requirement_groups.principle: Derogations from certain rights for public-interest archiving purposes
requirement_groups.requirement_summary: Where permitted by Union or Member State law, derogations from the rights to access, rectification, restriction, notification, portability, and objection may apply to processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, but only where those rights would seriously impair achieving the purpose, only to the extent necessary, and only alongside the 89(1) safeguards.
requirement_groups.applicability_condition: Applies only where the company relies on a public-interest-archiving derogation from data subject rights under applicable Union or Member State law.

sub_obligations.legal_text: Union or Member State law may provide for derogations from the rights referred to in Articles 15, 16, 18, 19, 20 and 21...in so far as such rights are likely to render impossible or seriously impair the achievement of the specific purposes, and such derogations are necessary for the fulfilment of those purposes
sub_obligations.plain_summary: Rights like access, rectification, restriction, notification, portability, and objection can only be limited for public-interest archiving if honoring them would seriously undermine the archiving and the limitation is necessary.
sub_obligations.evidence_prompt: Where the company limits data subject rights for public-interest archiving, does the policy confirm this is done only where such rights would seriously impair the specific purpose and only to the extent necessary, together with the safeguards required under 89(1)?

expected_evidence: Legal basis documentation citing applicable national archiving derogation law

assessment_rules.met_when: ALL sub-obligations are satisfied: any rights derogation for public-interest archiving is grounded in applicable law, limited to cases of serious impairment, necessary, and paired with 89(1) safeguards.
assessment_rules.partially_met_when: A derogation is applied but its legal basis, necessity, or accompanying safeguards are not clearly documented.
assessment_rules.not_met_when: Data subject rights are limited for public-interest archiving with no reference to a legal derogation or necessity test.
assessment_rules.conflicting_when: The policy applies a blanket denial of these rights to all archived data regardless of actual impact on the archiving purpose.
assessment_rules.insufficient_evidence_when: It is unclear whether the company applies any rights derogation for public-interest archiving.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Obligations of secrecy
article.contextual_reason: This article permits Member States to limit certain supervisory authority investigative powers (Article 58(1)(e) and (f)) toward controllers or processors bound by professional secrecy obligations, and requires notification of such rules to the Commission. It governs the scope of a regulator's powers under national law, not an affirmative obligation a company's privacy policy could satisfy or fail, so it is not testable against a company privacy policy.

chapter.name: Provisions relating to specific processing situations

article.title: Existing data protection rules of churches and religious associations
article.contextual_reason: This article addresses continuity of pre-existing comprehensive data protection rules maintained by churches and religious associations, and their supervision by an independent authority under Chapter VI. It applies to a narrow category of religious entities' institutional arrangements rather than general controller/processor obligations, and is not testable against a typical company's privacy policy.

article.title: Exercise of the delegation
article.contextual_reason: This article governs the European Commission's power to adopt delegated acts under Articles 12(8) and 43(8), including the delegation period, revocation by the European Parliament or Council, notification, and objection procedures. It is entirely an EU institutional law-making provision with no obligation directed at controllers or processors, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Committee procedure
article.contextual_reason: This article establishes that the Commission is assisted by a committee under Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 and specifies which comitology procedure (examination or advisory) applies when referenced elsewhere in the Regulation. It is a purely institutional/procedural provision for EU rule-making and imposes no obligation on controllers or processors, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Repeal of Directive 95/46/EC
article.contextual_reason: This article repeals the prior Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC as of 25 May 2018 and provides that references to it (and to the former Article 29 Working Party) are construed as references to the GDPR and the European Data Protection Board. It is a legislative transitional/interpretive provision with no obligation directed at controllers or processors, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Relationship with Directive 2002/58/EC
article.contextual_reason: This article clarifies that the GDPR does not impose additional obligations on providers of publicly available electronic communications services where the ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC) already imposes specific obligations with the same objective. It is a rule about which EU instrument governs a given matter (a conflict-of-laws/scoping provision), not an affirmative, independently testable requirement that a company's privacy policy would demonstrate compliance with — the underlying substantive obligations live in the ePrivacy Directive/national implementing law, not in this article itself.

article.title: Relationship with previously concluded Agreements
article.contextual_reason: This article preserves the validity of international transfer agreements concluded by Member States before 24 May 2016 that complied with the law applicable at that time, until they are amended, replaced, or revoked. It addresses Member State-level international agreements, not an obligation a typical company's privacy policy would document, so it is not testable in this context.

article.title: Commission reports
article.contextual_reason: This article requires the European Commission to periodically evaluate and report on the Regulation's application (particularly Chapters V and VII) to the European Parliament and Council, and to propose amendments if necessary. It is a Commission reporting and legislative-review duty, not a controller or processor obligation, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Review of other Union legal acts on data protection
article.contextual_reason: This article directs the Commission to propose amendments to other EU legal acts on data protection to ensure consistent protection, particularly regarding processing by EU institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. It is a Commission legislative-review duty, not a controller or processor obligation, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.

article.title: Entry into force and application
article.contextual_reason: This article sets the Regulation's entry-into-force date and its application date of 25 May 2018, and confirms it is binding and directly applicable in all Member States. It is a purely legislative/temporal provision with no substantive obligation for controllers or processors to demonstrate compliance with in a policy, so it cannot be tested against a company privacy policy.
